Dissemble
di-SEM-bl
verb
From the Old French dissimuler, from the Latin dissimulare, “to make unlike, to disguise, to feign that a thing is not what it is” (from dis-, “not,” and similis, “like”); hence to hide under a false appearance, to play the part of what one is not.

Biblical Definition

To dissemble is to disguise the truth by acting a part — not the blunt lie of the mouth only, but the lie of the whole man, the false face that makes a thing seem what it is not. Achan’s theft is charged so: Israel “have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff” (Jos 7:11). The wedge of gold hid in the tent was covered by a face that stood among the tribes as though nothing were amiss. Solomon marks the same craft in speech: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him” (Pro 26:24) — hatred is smooth outside and stores its poison within. The word’s gravest hour is at Antioch. Peter, who had eaten freely with the Gentiles, withdrew when certain came from James, fearing them of the circumcision; “and the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation” (Gal 2:13). Not one word of false doctrine was preached — only a chair moved, a table left — yet the act denied justification by faith alone, and the contagion carried off even Barnabas. So Paul “withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11), publicly, before them all. Here is the rule the church must keep: where the truth of the gospel is at stake, the apostle would not spare an apostle. Dissembling is never a small thing, for it preaches with the body what the mouth would never dare say.

Webster 1828 Definition

To hide under a false appearance; to feign; to act a part contrary to the truth of the thing.

DISSEMBLE, to hide under a false appearance; to conceal the real fact or motive.

From the Latin dissimulare, “to make unlike, to feign.”

Achan stole and dissembled, the false face covering the accursed thing (Jos 7:11).

He that hateth dissembleth with his lips and layeth up deceit within (Pro 26:24).

At Antioch Peter and the Jews dissembled, and even Barnabas was carried away (Gal 2:13).

Key Scripture

Gal 2:11 — "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

Gal 2:13 — "And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation."

Jos 7:11 — "Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff."

Pro 26:24 — "He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;"

Modern Corruption

A live and pressing corruption: the age calls dissembling kindness, and a winsome cowardice that will not name error is Antioch over again.

expand to see more

The corruption is not in the word but in our practice of the thing, and it wears a pleasant name. Peter at Antioch preached no heresy; he simply withdrew from the Gentile table when the men of the circumcision came in, and by that quiet courtesy he denied with his feet the gospel he had confessed with his mouth. Our own dissembling is the same: the minister who will not say from the pulpit what he believes in the study, the man who softens the doctrine to keep the room warm, the church that calls its silence winsomeness. It is dissimulation, and Barnabas himself — the son of consolation, Paul’s own companion — was carried away with it. Cowardice in the pulpit is contagious; it never stops with the coward.

Paul’s answer is the standing rule: he “withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed,” and he did it before them all. Gospel clarity outranks ecclesiastical politeness. Where justification by faith alone is at stake, the deference owed to a great name is owed no longer, for the truth of the gospel is not Peter’s property nor Paul’s but Christ’s. Achan’s dissembling hid a wedge of gold and cost Israel a battle and a valley of trouble; the dissembling at Antioch would have hidden the cross itself. Better an open rebuke that saves the church than a smooth face that damns it, for he that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and he that loves speaks plainly.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to hide the truth under a false appearance, to feign what one is not.

expand to see more

Dissemble — Old French dissimuler, from Latin dissimulare.

From dis-, “not,” and similis, “like” — to make a thing unlike itself.

It denotes the lie of the whole man, not of the tongue only.

Achan stole and dissembled, hiding the accursed thing (Jos 7:11).

Peter’s dissimulation at Antioch drew Paul’s open rebuke (Gal 2:11-13).

Usage

"Achan dissembled: the wedge lay in the tent while his face stood innocent among the tribes."

"Peter dissembled at Antioch by moving a chair, and denied with his feet what he confessed with his lips."

"Paul withstood him to the face — gospel clarity outranks every politeness owed to a great name."
